title: Preclinical evaluation of NHC and molnupiravir against severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus.
abstract: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an emerging tick-borne zoonotic disease caused by severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV). The disease can be severe or fatal in companion animals. In veterinary medicine, no specific treatment has been established for SFTS, and management is limited to supportive care. To investigate the antiviral potential of molnupiravir against SFTSV, we evaluated the activity of its ribonucleoside metabolite, β-D-N 4 -hydroxycytidine (NHC), in feline- and canine-derived cells and the effects of oral molnupiravir on survival and blood viral RNA loads in a lethal mouse model. NHC inhibited the production of infectious SFTSV in all four cell lines tested, with plaque assay-based 50% effective concentrations of 0.33-0.97 μM. In SFTSV-infected mice lacking type I and type II interferon receptors, oral molnupiravir treatment (100 mg/kg twice daily for 3 days), initiated at 24, 48, or 72 h post-infection, delayed mortality and reduced median blood viral RNA loads. However, only one of six mice in each treated group survived to 12 days post-infection. At 6 days post-infection, median blood viral RNA loads in treated groups were 0.57%-1.59% of the median load in vehicle controls, with significant reductions when treatment was initiated at 24 or 48 h. In a separate experiment, extending treatment to 5 or 7 days did not demonstrate a clear additional survival benefit. These findings demonstrate antiviral activity in companion animal-derived cells and delayed mortality in an interferon-receptor-deficient mouse model. Further studies are required to establish therapeutic efficacy in naturally infected cats.

title: Platelet-derived extracellular vesicles aggravate macrophagic pyroptosis in Dabie bandavirus infection
abstract: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an emerging tick-borne infectious disease causing remarkably increased morbidity and mortality in East Asia. Thrombocytopenia is a hallmark pathogenic event in SFTS, clinical feature and an independent predictor of multi-organ failure and poor clinical outcomes. Although Dabie bandavirus (DBV) can bind to and replicate within platelets, the contribution of activated platelets to SFTS pathogenesis remains elusive. Here, we identify platelet-derived extracellular vesicles induced by DBV (DPEVs) as critical mediators of immune dysregulation. DBV-activated platelets released abundant extracellular vesicles that directly induced macrophage pyroptosis and markedly amplified virus-driven inflammatory responses. Proteomic and functional analyses demonstrated that DPEVs reprogram macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory and pyroptosis-prone state. Compared with vesicles generated by physical disruption, DPEVs displayed enhanced immunostimulatory capacity, indicating stimulus-dependent functional specialization. Mechanistically, DPEVs disrupted mitochondrial integrity, promoted mitochondrial reactive oxygen species production, thereby triggering the downstream pyroptotic program. In addition, DPEVs were capable of incorporating viral components, suggesting a potential dual role in both inflammatory amplification and viral dissemination. Collectively, these findings define a previously unrecognized pathogenic axis linking platelet activation, extracellular vesicle signaling, mitochondrial injury, and macrophage pyroptosis during DBV infection. DPEVs act as a key amplifier of inflammation and provide a mechanistic link between thrombocytopenia and disease severity in SFTS, highlighting their potential value as both biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

title_zh: 血小板源性细胞外囊泡加重大别班达病毒感染的巨噬细胞焦亡
source_body_en: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an emerging tick-borne infectious disease causing remarkably increased morbidity and mortality in East Asia. Thrombocytopenia is a hallmark pathogenic event in SFTS, clinical feature and an independent predictor of multi-organ failure and poor clinical outcomes. Although Dabie bandavirus (DBV) can bind to and replicate within platelets, the contribution of activated platelets to SFTS pathogenesis remains elusive. Here, we identify platelet-derived extracellular vesicles induced by DBV (DPEVs) as critical mediators of immune dysregulation. DBV-activated platelets released abundant extracellular vesicles that directly induced macrophage pyroptosis and markedly amplified virus-driven inflammatory responses. Proteomic and functional analyses demonstrated that DPEVs reprogram macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory and pyroptosis-prone state. Compared with vesicles generated by physical disruption, DPEVs displayed enhanced immunostimulatory capacity, indicating stimulus-dependent functional specialization. Mechanistically, DPEVs disrupted mitochondrial integrity, promoted mitochondrial reactive oxygen species production, thereby triggering the downstream pyroptotic program. In addition, DPEVs were capable of incorporating viral components, suggesting a potential dual role in both inflammatory amplification and viral dissemination. Collectively, these findings define a previously unrecognized pathogenic axis linking platelet activation, extracellular vesicle signaling, mitochondrial injury, and macrophage pyroptosis during DBV infection. DPEVs act as a key amplifier of inflammation and provide a mechanistic link between thrombocytopenia and disease severity in SFTS, highlighting their potential value as both biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

title: Seasonality of Haemaphysalis longicornis and its implications for the transmission of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus: a modelling study
abstract: Background The Asian longhorned tick, Haemaphysalis longicornis, is the primary vector of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), an emerging infectious disease rapidly spreading in Asia with a case-fatality rate of up to 30%. Understanding the seasonal activity of H. longicornis is critical for elucidating SFTS epidemiology and improving risk prediction. Methods We compiled databases of life stage-specific seasonal activity data for H. longicornis, as well as laboratory-derived developmental durations under different temperature conditions, from the published literature. We then developed an empirical model integrating laboratory observations with field temperature data to predict interstadial and full-generation developmental durations across 20 locations with observed tick seasonality, seven SFTS transmission hotspots, and three locations without reported H. longicornis presence. Finally, we inferred the cohort structures underlying observed H. longicornis seasonal patterns by integrating observed seasonality with model-predicted developmental durations. Results Despite substantial variation in annual mean temperature (7.3–17.4°C), the seasonal activity of H. longicornis was largely synchronous across locations, with nymphs peaking in spring, adults in summer, larvae in fall, and no detectable activity during winter, potentially attributable to the substantially higher overwinter survival of nymphs than of other life stages. In contrast, human SFTS cases exhibited diverse seasonal patterns, with peaks occurring in May, July, or October depending on the location, suggesting that variation in human-tick contact patterns may play an important role in shaping the observed seasonality of human SFTS. The predicted full-generation developmental duration was 1–2 years in locations with observed H. longicornis seasonality or reported human SFTS cases, but < 1 year in locations without known H. longicornis presence under most examined scenarios. Inferred cohort structures showed that a single seasonal activity peak may comprise multiple overlapping cohorts. For example, the summer adult peak from May to August likely consists of overwintered adults for the early part, and newly matured adults that fed as nymphs in the spring for the latter part. Conclusions These findings highlight the need to consider human-tick contact patterns and location- and month-specific temporal scales when modelling human SFTS risk.

title: A novel 17-plex multi-pathogen detection for rapid and accurate diagnosis of tick-borne diseases
abstract: In recent years, anthropogenic ecological disruption has escalated tick-borne zoonoses; ticks transmit taxonomically diverse pathogens with overlapping clinical signs, challenging precise diagnosis and increasing risk of simultaneous detection in pooled samples. Despite advancements, current sequencing technologies, such as Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS), Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) assays, and antibody-based detection methods, are hampered by limitations including extended processing times and limited detection throughput. These constraints significantly hinder their effectiveness in high-throughput pathogen screening for animal or patient samples. To address these challenges, we developed an innovative multi-detection method based on the Multi-analyte Suspension Assay (MASA), enabling rapid and accurate diagnosis of a comprehensive panel of 17 vector-borne pathogens. This 17-plex panel comprises Rickettsia spp., Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Borrelia recurrentis, Babesia spp., Borrelia burgdorferi, Rickettsia prowazekii, Rickettsia heilongjiangensis, Orientia tsutsugamushi, Coxiella burnetii, Leptospira, Bartonella spp., Candidatus Ehrlichia erytraense, Hantaan Virus (HTNV), Seoul Virus (SEOV), Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus (CCHFV), Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome Virus (SFTSV), and Tick-Borne Encephalitis Virus (TBEV). By combining this novel method with traditional techniques, including nested PCR and Real-Time Quantitative Reverse Transcription PCR (qRT-PCR), we achieved accurate detection of pathogens such as Rickettsia spp., Anaplasma phagocytophilum, and SFTSV in tick samples. Notably, the technique revealed the co-existence of multiple pathogens within the same sample group, highlighting its ability in identifying co-detection of pathogens. Additionally, in suspected cases of tick-borne pathogen infection in febrile patients, the method quickly identified positive results for SFTSV and Rickettsia spp. These preliminary results suggest the potential of this method as a promising screening tool for clinical diagnostics, although larger-scale validation is warranted. This method provides a preliminary technical candidate approach for the development of more sensitive field-deployable detection tools.

source_records.abstract: In recent years, anthropogenic ecological disruption has escalated tick-borne zoonoses; ticks transmit taxonomically diverse pathogens with overlapping clinical signs, challenging precise diagnosis and increasing risk of simultaneous detection in pooled samples. Despite advancements, current sequencing technologies, such as Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS), Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) assays, and antibody-based detection methods, are hampered by limitations including extended processing times and limited detection throughput. These constraints significantly hinder their effectiveness in high-throughput pathogen screening for animal or patient samples. To address these challenges, we developed an innovative multi-detection method based on the Multi-analyte Suspension Assay (MASA), enabling rapid and accurate diagnosis of a comprehensive panel of 17 vector-borne pathogens. This 17-plex panel comprises Rickettsia spp., Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Borrelia recurrentis, Babesia spp., Borrelia burgdorferi, Rickettsia prowazekii, Rickettsia heilongjiangensis, Orientia tsutsugamushi, Coxiella burnetii, Leptospira, Bartonella spp., Candidatus Ehrlichia erytraense, Hantaan Virus (HTNV), Seoul Virus (SEOV), Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus (CCHFV), Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome Virus (SFTSV), and Tick-Borne Encephalitis Virus (TBEV). By combining this novel method with traditional techniques, including nested PCR and Real-Time Quantitative Reverse Transcription PCR (qRT-PCR), we achieved accurate detection of pathogens such as Rickettsia spp., Anaplasma phagocytophilum, and SFTSV in tick samples. Notably, the technique revealed the co-existence of multiple pathogens within the same sample group, highlighting its ability in identifying co-detection of pathogens. This method provides a preliminary technical candidate approach for the development of more sensitive field-deployable detection tools.

title: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome-associated viral sepsis: risk factors for critical illness and mortality and the prognostic value of urinalysis
abstract: Background Since its identification in China in 2009, severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) has emerged as an important tick-borne pathogen associated with substantial severity and mortality. Early recognition of patients at high risk of clinical deterioration or death remains challenging, particularly in resource-limited settings. Methods In this retrospective multicenter study, 798 patients with laboratory-confirmed SFTSV infection were included, who were admitted to five tertiary hospitals in Jiangsu and Anhui provinces, China, between April 1, 2021, to October 31, 2024. Patients were classified as critical (n=271) or non-critical (n=527), and critically ill patients were further categorized as survivors (n=134) or non-survivors (n=137). Demographic characteristics, comorbidities, clinical manifestations, organ dysfunction, hematological and coagulation indices, biochemical markers, urinalysis findings, and arterial blood gas parameters were evaluated. Urinalysis included urinary protein, occult blood, glucose, bilirubin, urobilinogen, pH, and urinary red and white blood cell counts, among other routine parameters. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify factors independently associated with critical illness and in-hospital mortality. Results Of 798 patients with SFTSV infection, 271 (34.0%) developed critical illness, of whom 137 (50.6%) died during hospitalization. The median age was 67 years [interquartile range (IQR) 58-73], and 87.3% resided in rural areas. Compared with non-critical patients, critically ill patients exhibited more pronounced hematological and coagulation abnormalities, biochemical evidence of organ injury, and urinary abnormalities, particularly proteinuria, hematuria, and glycosuria. Multivariable analysis identified age, neurological, renal, and respiratory dysfunction, direct bilirubin, alanine aminotransferase (ALT), creatine kinase (CK) and D-dimer as independent factors associated with critical illness. Among critically ill patients, non-survivors had greater organ dysfunction and higher illness severity scores than survivors. Notably, urinalysis revealed a significantly higher frequency of urobilinogen positivity (25.5% vs. 13.4%, p = 0.012) and elevated urinary white blood cell (WBC) counts in non-survivors. Multivariable analysis further identified age, urinary urobilinogen positivity, and creatinine, as independent factors associated with in-hospital mortality. These findings suggest that selected urinary abnormalities may provide complementary information for mortality risk assessment in critically ill patients with SFTS. Conclusion SFTSV infection is a systemic disease characterized by profound hematological and coagulation disturbances together with progressive multiorgan dysfunction. Age, neurological, renal, and respiratory dysfunction and biochemical markers of organ injury were independently associated with critical illness, whereas advanced age and selected urinary abnormalities were independently associated with mortality among critically ill patients. These findings support comprehensive early assessment of organ dysfunction and routine laboratory and urinalysis monitoring for risk stratification and clinical management of SFTS.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates risk factors for critical illness and mortality in patients with severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) infection. It highlights the importance of early recognition of high-risk patients, particularly in resource-limited settings, and identifies age, neurological, renal, and respiratory dysfunction, along with specific biochemical and urinalysis markers, as independent predictors of critical illness and mortality. The findings suggest that urinary abnormalities, such as urobilinogen positivity and elevated white blood cell counts, may offer additional insights for risk assessment in critically ill SFTSV patients. The study is a retrospective multicenter analysis of 798 patients admitted to hospitals in Jiangsu and Anhui provinces between 2021 and 2024. While the study provides valuable insights into the clinical features and prognostic indicators of SFTSV, it does not report specific limitations, which may affect the confidence in its conclusions.

title: LPC(16:0) and prothrombin time as mortality predictors in severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome
abstract: ABSTRACT Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an emerging tick-borne viral disease with a high fatality rate. However, the impact of the SFTS virus (SFTSV) on host lipid metabolism and its relationship with the prognosis of patients remain unclear. To determine the lipid metabolism profile of SFTSV-infected and identify prognostic biomarkers, targeted lipidomics analysis was conducted on SFTSV-infected Huh7 cells and serum samples from 71 subjects (including 15 healthy controls, 35 SFTS survivors, and 21 SFTS deceased patients) in this study. Our findings revealed that glycerophospholipid metabolism was the most significantly disrupted pathway in both SFTSV-infected Huh7 cells and SFTS patients, with lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) species, including LPC(16:1), LPC(18:1), LPC(16:0), and LPC(18:0), showing decreased levels. Together with clinical parameters, prothrombin time (PT) and LPC(16:0) were further identified as prognostic factors, and the combined model incorporating these two markers predicted mortality with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.937. These findings provide a foundation for mortality prediction and mechanistic understanding of SFTS. IMPORTANCE Effective prognostic tools and targeted therapies for SFTS remain urgently needed, as current clinical management relies largely on supportive care and lacks reliable indicators for early risk stratification. This study enhances our understanding of lipid alterations following SFTSV infection, opens potential avenues for metabolism-targeted intervention, and may aid in assessing disease progression and guiding appropriate clinical interventions.

To determine the lipid metabolism profile of SFTSV-infected and identify prognostic biomarkers, targeted lipidomics analysis was conducted on SFTSV-infected Huh7 cells and serum samples from 71 subjects (including 15 healthy controls, 35 SFTS survivors, and 21 SFTS deceased patients) in this study. Our findings revealed that glycerophospholipid metabolism was the most significantly disrupted pathway in both SFTSV-infected Huh7 cells and SFTS patients, with lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) species, including LPC(16:1), LPC(18:1), LPC(16:0), and LPC(18:0), showing decreased levels. Together with clinical parameters, prothrombin time (PT) and LPC(16:0) were further identified as prognostic factors, and the combined model incorporating these two markers predicted mortality with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.937. These findings provide a foundation for mortality prediction and mechanistic understanding of SFTS. IMPORTANCE Effective prognostic tools and targeted therapies for SFTS remain urgently needed, as current clinical management relies largely on supportive care and lacks reliable indicators for early risk stratification. This study enhances our understanding of lipid alterations following SFTSV infection, opens potential avenues for metabolism-targeted intervention, and may aid in assessing disease progression and guiding appropriate clinical interventions.

title: Genetic Diversity and Evidence of Reassortment of Crimean–Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus in Ghana
abstract: Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a tick-borne zoonotic virus with a wide distribution and significant genetic variation, driven in part by reassortment of genome segments. Despite increased transmission throughout Africa, genetic data on CCHFV diversity and reassortment are scarce. This study evaluated ticks sampled from slaughtered cattle at the Kumasi abattoir for CCHFV. Ticks were morphologically identified and screened using RT-qPCR targeting the S segment, followed by whole-genome sequencing of positive samples. Amblyomma variegatum accounted for 65% of the 768 ticks collected in 2020. CCHFV was detected in two ticks (0.26%), including one Hyalomma truncatum (0.13%) and one Hyalomma rufipes (0.13%). A full genome obtained from H. rufipes was compared to previously described Ghanaian strains. Phylogenetic analyzes revealed that the S and L segments belonged to Genotype III (Africa 3), which corresponded to strains from Ghana and West Africa, while the M segment belonged to Genotype I (Africa 1), which was closely related to a strain previously detected at the Navrongo abattoir. Likelihood-based topology analyses indicated significant divergence between the M and S/L segment phylogenies, supporting genome segment reassortment. The findings show that CCHFV circulates in Ghanaian ticks and that reassortment occurs, emphasizing the importance of comprehensive One Health genomic surveillance to track viral evolution and rising public health risks.

title: A structural atlas of antibody-reactive regions in the Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus nucleoprotein
abstract: Abstract Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is an emerging zoonotic pathogen for which serological surveillance remains essential to detect human exposure and circulation in animals. The viral nucleoprotein (Np) is the principal antigen used in antibody-based assays because of its abundance, immunogenicity, and conservation. Numerous Np-reactive fragments and epitopes have been reported in humans, livestock, laboratory animals, and monoclonal antibody studies, yet the structural organization of the CCHFV Np antibody response is not available. In this study, we integrate the available epitope-mapping literature into a unified structural and sequence-level framework. Reported linear fragments and epitopes were projected onto the Np sequence of the CCHFV Hoti strain, mapped onto the available Np structure, and summarized as residue-level epitope density. This antigenic map was compared with sequence entropy and conservation to relate recurrently targeted regions to sequence variability and identify residues not represented in the experimental crystal structure. The resulting atlas reveals that Np immunoreactivity is distributed across both the head and stalk subdomains, but is organized into recurrent hotspots rather than a diffuse surface. The stalk-associated region emerges as a recurrently recognized antigenic region across the available studies. Importantly, the sequence-level analysis also identifies regions with epitope or variability signal that are not represented in the crystallographic structure, emphasizing the value of combining three-dimensional mapping with full-length sequence tracks. By consolidating scattered epitope information into an integrated antigenic landscape, this work provides a practical reference for CCHFV serology, comparative humoral immunology, and the design of improved Np-based diagnostic antigens.

title: Serological Evidence of Exposure to Crimean‐Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus in Equids in Spain
abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction Crimean‐Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is an emerging tick‐borne zoonotic pathogen in western Europe, with established circulation in Spain. Although wildlife hosts are known to contribute to virus maintenance, the role of domestic species, including equids, remains poorly understood. This study aimed to assess serological reactivity against CCHFV in equids in endemic regions of Spain. Methods A total of 494 equids, including 430 horses ( Equus caballus ), 54 mules ( Equus mulus ) and 10 donkeys ( Equus asinus ) were analyzed. Samples were screened with a commercial double‐antigen multispecies ELISA and all ELISA‐reactive sera, together with a subset of ELISA‐negative sera, were tested by virus neutralization test (VNT). Results Eleven of 494 animals were ELISA‐reactive (apparent ELISA seroprevalence 2.2%; 95% CI: 1.1–3.9), comprising 7 horses (1.6%; 95% CI: 0.7–3.3) and 4 mules (7.4%; 95% CI: 2.1–17.9); no reactive donkeys were detected (0%; 95% CI: 0–30.8). Reactive animals originated exclusively from Andalucía (10/184; 5.4%) and Castilla‐La Mancha (1/90; 1.1%). title: CRISPR-Cas9 Knockout Screen Identifies “Arsenical Pump-Driving ATPase Protein” as a Novel Host Factor Supporting Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus Infection
abstract: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a zoonotic pathogen with high mortality and limited therapeutic options, and listed as a priority pathogen in the WHO's R&D Blueprint. Using a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen, we identified Arsenical pump-driving ATPase protein (ASNA-1/TRC40) as a novel host factor required for CCHFV infection. Knockout of ASNA-1 leads to a significant inhibition of viral replication across multiple clinical isolates of CCHFV, spanning diverse geographic clades. Furthermore, the small-molecule inhibitor Retro-2.1, which targets ASNA-1/TRC40 in the Transmembrane Domain Recognition Complex (TRC) pathway, potently inhibits CCHFV replication without significant cytotoxicity. Our findings demonstrate that ASNA-1 is essential for the CCHFV life cycle and establish the ASNA-1/TRC40 pathway as a viable, broad-spectrum target for antiviral intervention against this neglected and lethal human pathogen.

full_text: nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2357–2359 | 2357 Vaccine preparedness for the next emerging infectious disease crisis Florian Krammer Recent outbreaks with viruses such as Bundi­bugyo virus and Andes virus are a reminder that another pandemic can happen at any time. This Comment summarizes where we stand with pandemic preparedness from a vaccine perspective. During the COVID-19 pandemic, we witnessed vaccine develop­ment at its finest. Vaccines against the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 were developed at record speed and were made available within approximately 1 year after the outbreak started1. This swift devel­ opment of vaccines was facilitated by new technologies such as the mRNA vaccine platform2 but also by a wealth of exist­ ing knowledge because of many years of virology, vacci­nology and structural biology research. Much has happened since the COVID-19 pandemic. Technology has evolved, new insights into mechanisms of protection and basic immunology have been gained and regulatory and policy views have changed (Fig. 1), especially in the USA. Where does this leave us with vaccine preparedness for emerging pathogens? Mucosal immunity matters A clear lesson learned from the COVID-19 pandemic was that intramus­ cular vaccination can only imperfectly protect from infection with respiratory viruses per se and from onward transmission1. Vaccines that are administered via mucosal surfaces may be a better option to induce immunity in the upper respiratory tract to protect from infection with respiratory viruses. However, there is much still to learn; from basic research and clinical testing to manufacturing and regulatory policies. The study is based on a review of existing knowledge and current vaccine technologies, and it identifies limitations in the current state of vaccine development for emerging pathogens. The evidence is strong due to its focus on well-documented experiences and policy changes, but the commentary does not present original data.

analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,粘膜 疫苗 可以提供更好的针对呼吸道病毒的保护,他们强调了认识粘膜免疫在大流行防范中重要性的新颖性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,具有既定功效和安全性的粘膜 疫苗 可以增强人们对这些平台的信心,并在未来的 疫苗 或大流行期间实现更快的部署。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于评论,不提供原始数据,但由于其重点关注了来自 COVID-19 大流行和当前 疫苗 发展趋势的有据可查的经验教训,因此证据有力。
